title: How university students pick their classes
author: Matt Ely
summary: Matt Ely, a part-time undergraduate advisor at Indiana University, walks through the three data tools students actually use to pick classes at a large university: the school's own Grade Distribution site (past grade breakdowns by instructor and section), the OCQ Dashboard (aggregated student course-evaluation survey results), and the external, unofficial Rate My Professor. His framing device is that a school the size of IU (over 3,000 undergraduate courses at Bloomington alone) creates two simultaneous information problems: a near-total deficiency of qualitative, word-of-mouth knowledge about any given course, and an overabundance of quantitative data that the university makes easy to search but that answers only proxy questions. He walks through a running example (three introductory religion courses) to show how a student can quickly rank options by recommendation rate and workload using the official tools, then supplement with Rate My Professor for the qualitative color the official data withholds. Ely's real argument surfaces at the end: none of these metrics -- grades, time-on-task, likability -- actually answers the question a student is trying to ask, which is whether a course is good, and the scale of a modern university makes that harder to answer, not easier, even as it makes proxy data more available than ever. The piece functions as a case study in how information architecture, rather than course content itself, ends up driving student choice.
points: Ely's key structural insight is the mismatch between two data problems at scale: too little qualitative information about any single course, paired with too much quantitative data that the university has made trivially searchable -- and neither one actually answers what students want to know.

He shows the tools compound rather than replace each other: students triangulate grade distributions, aggregated OCQ satisfaction scores, and a much smaller, more emotionally-loaded set of Rate My Professor reviews, each filling a gap the others leave open.

His closing move reframes the whole piece as an epistemics problem, not a data-availability problem: metrics like grade percentage, time-on-task, and likability are all measurable proxies for course quality, but none of them is course quality, and no amount of additional data resolves that gap.

The Rate My Professor comparison quietly demonstrates a selection-bias mechanism worth flagging to any reader building their own course-evaluation tools: a site with only 51 voluntary reviews (versus 808 mandatory ones) skews toward stronger feelings in both directions, not a representative sample.
quotes: Selecting courses is a challenge no matter how large your institution is. There's always an element of mystery to a class not yet conducted. All students rely on hearsay, reputation, and impression to some degree.

The first is a deficiency of qualitative data. There are so many courses at the university, that no student (and no advisor) can expect to have even secondhand information about most of them. This semester, IU is offering over 3,000 undergraduate courses at its Bloomington campus.
They want to know which instructor gave 47% of their students an A and which gave an A to just 12%.
But that's not all OCQ can do. You can compare the results of different instructors in one class. You can also compare different courses.
The recommendation rate is much lower here than on OCQ. As expected, voluntarily completing a report on this site tends to draw on people with stronger feelings, both positive and negative.

These kinds of questions are related to course quality, but none of them completely answer an essential question: Is this a good class? We can't agree on what "good" means. So we use shorthands like "easy" or "fun.
The scale of university education makes asking the essential question difficult and answering it impossible.
